doc.title: Yusef Lateef — Smithsonian Jazz Oral History

title: Switching to tenor after hearing Lester Young
summary: Why he moved from alto to tenor in 1939 and what he loved in Lester Young's poetic use of silence compared with Hawkins.

story.theme_name: Lester Young: the man, the sound, the Basie years
story.community_name: Remembering Lester Young: Prez the man and his sound

blocks.x: Now, when you’re uh–going back to, to Detroit here, are you primarily playing alto when you’re enrolled at Wayne State? Had you started with tenor?
Well, you know, I only played alto for one year...
...The first year, and then I heard Lester Young. That’s how I, I started on tenor in 1939.
So many musicians uh...hearing Lester Young was such a water shed for so many people. Tell us what uh...what you fell in love with when you heard Lester Young.

Um...I suppose I can say it was his ability to sound so poetic, uh...to express such warmth and depth of feeling, and that’s what attracted me. And the interventions of of non-saxophone sounds, perhaps, you could say, that he articulated with cross- fingerings, et cetera.
No, I think that’s, that’s certainly true, and that’s something that seemed to grow more sublime with him as he uh, as he progressed.
Yeah, and his, the way he utilizes, utilized silence was, was unique. Uh...opposed...differ–a contrasting style would be Coleman Hawkins, who, he, who was a master, also.

Of course. He uh, Coleman Hawkins would, would play mini-notes and, that were meaningful, but Lester Young would be play fewer notes, and there would be silence which would give you time to digest, I think I can say, what had gone before.
He was a master at that. He expressed that in D.B. Blues.
[scatting the melody] You can hear the silence.
